It received FDA accelerated approval in September 2025 for Barth syndrome, with a confirmatory trial ongoing.

peptides.name: Kisspeptin
peptides.shortSummary: A reproductive neuropeptide under active clinical research, not an approved therapy.

A randomized study published in August 2026 reported an intermittent administration schedule that sustained gonadotropin secretion over 12 days in healthy men, addressing a longstanding desensitization problem. It remains investigational.

news.summary: Thirty-three days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides - BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax - for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the agency's compounding file is unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six appears in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed without a date or docket. What moved this period is where the evidence debate is being held: a narrative review by pain-medicine physicians at Brigham and Women's Hospital formally surveyed BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and related regenerative peptides for chronic pain and reached much the same verdict as FDA's own July briefing documents - plausible mechanisms, extensive preclinical data, thin human evidence, and unapproved status. The approved GLP-1 medicines, by contrast, keep producing large human and economic datasets: an industry-authored matched cohort of adults over 55 reported healthcare-cost offsets on tirzepatide growing to about 25 percent by 12-18 months, a spine-surgery meta-analysis found procedure-specific rather than class-wide signals for bone fusion after cervical spine surgery, and a scoping review counted 21 studies - most preclinical - on incretin drugs in opioid use disorder. FDA's separate April 2026 proposal to permanently exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list continues through its process. None of the six recommended peptides may lawfully be compounded today. This is general research, not medical advice.

items: Semaglutide — Ozempic (2017), Wegovy (2021), Rybelsus (2019); type 2 diabetes & obesity.
Tirzepatide — Mounjaro (2022), Zepbound (2023); type 2 diabetes & obesity.
Liraglutide — Victoza (2010), Saxenda (2014); type 2 diabetes & obesity.
Tesamorelin — Egrifta (2010); HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
PT-141 / Bremelanotide — Vyleesi (2019); HSDD in premenopausal women.
Sermorelin — formerly FDA-approved (Geref, discontinued as a branded product); now supplied mainly via compounding pharmacies.
Elamipretide / SS-31 — Forzinity (FDA accelerated approval, Sep 2025); Barth syndrome — the first mitochondria-targeted therapy. Confirmatory Phase 3b/4 (4TAZPower) ongoing.

Orforglipron — Foundayo (FDA approval, 1 Apr 2026); chronic weight management. A once-daily oral SMALL-MOLECULE GLP-1 receptor agonist, not a peptide — listed for context because it now competes directly with the injectable peptide GLP-1s. 52-week Phase 3 safety in Japanese adults with type 2 diabetes (ACHIEVE-J, NCT06010004) published Aug 2026.

Retatrutide — GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist; Phase 3 complete, sponsor states a Biologics License Application is planned for Q1 2027; a narrow expanded-access (compassionate use) programme was confirmed by the sponsor on 3 Aug 2026 — physician-initiated, and still requiring FDA and IRB authorisation. Not approved anywhere.

Cagrilintide / CagriSema — amylin analog (± semaglutide); Phase 3; under regulatory development; Aug 2026: sponsor's Q2 report disclosed a head-to-head Phase 3 in which CagriSema controlled blood sugar less well than tirzepatide.
Amycretin (zenagamtide) — GLP-1/amylin co-agonist (oral & injectable); Phase 3; head-to-head Phase 3 vs semaglutide in obesity registered Jul 2026 (AMAZE 7, NCT07668414).

Compounding reclassification (a compounding decision, not a drug approval): at its July 23–24, 2026 meeting the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted to recommend adding six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon, and Semax — to the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, and voted against Emideltide (DSIP). The votes overrode FDA's own briefing recommendation, are advisory only, and any listing now depends on FDA notice-and-comment rulemaking. See Recent Headlines for the outcome and RFK Jr. / HHS context.

Next compounding review (scheduling stage, not a drug approval): FDA has posted an early announcement for a further PCAC meeting before the end of February 2027 to consider five more substances for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List — Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II, and Mechano Growth Factor, Pegylated (PEG-MGF). Date, docket, and briefing materials are not yet published.
Approved abroad but NOT by the US FDA: Thymosin Alpha-1 (thymalfasin/Zadaxin — many countries), Selank (Russia), Semax (Russia), GHRP-2 / pralmorelin (diagnostic use, Japan).

Restricted abroad: Health Canada has not authorised BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, TB-500 or retatrutide as injectable drugs, warns against unauthorised peptides sold online, and obtained a permanent injunction against a Canadian retailer in June 2026.

Investigational / sold as research chemicals (US, not approved): CJC-1295, Ipamorelin, GHK-Cu (sold as a cosmetic ingredient), LL-37, Melanotan II, DSIP, Dihexa, Pinealon, AOD-9604, GHRP-6, Hexarelin, IGF-1 LR3, Kisspeptin.

Tirzepatide (new indication) — first randomised trial of tirzepatide as an adjunct to buprenorphine for opioid use disorder (TAB, NIH Clinical Trials Network, 9 sites, ~310 participants); protocol published Aug 2026, no results yet. Tirzepatide is FDA approved for type 2 diabetes and obesity only. A Phase 4 randomised trial of resistance training versus usual care during tirzepatide treatment, with thigh muscle volume as the primary outcome, was registered 17 Aug 2026 (NCT07777575, Technical University of Munich, 150 participants). A Phase 1 trial of tirzepatide for lorlatinib-associated weight gain in non-small-cell lung cancer was registered 22 Aug 2026 (NCT07782359, University of Chicago, 30 participants).

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 33 after the PCAC vote — the file is still frozen, but academic pain medicine has started formally reviewing the same peptides FDA is weighing
timeline.content: Thirty-three days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted at its 23-24 July 2026 meeting to recommend six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the regulatory ledger remains unchanged: no proposed rule, no Federal Register notice, none of the six in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and no date or docket for the further PCAC meeting flagged for Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF. Today's angle is where the evidence debate is happening instead: the academic clinic. A narrative review published this week in Current Pain and Headache Reports by anesthesiology and pain-medicine physicians at Brigham and Women's Hospital formally surveys BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and related regenerative peptides for chronic pain management — the first time several of these compounds have been systematically treated in a mainstream pain journal — and reaches essentially the same verdict as FDA's own briefing documents did in July: mechanisms are plausible, preclinical data are extensive, human evidence is thin, and most of the agents are unapproved. That convergence matters because the PCAC votes ran against FDA's briefing assessment, and the eventual rulemaking will have to weigh the same literature these clinician-reviewers describe as limited. Meanwhile the approved side of the ledger keeps generating economic and surgical datasets — an industry-authored cost analysis in adults over 55 and a spine-surgery meta-analysis both published this week (see below) — and FDA's separate April 2026 proposal to permanently exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list continues through its process. None of the six recommended peptides may lawfully be compounded today. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA PCAC meeting page](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [Curr Pain Headache Rep](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11916-026-01542-z), [Pharmacy Times](https://www.pharmacytimes.com/view/fda-moves-to-permanently-close-the-door-on-compounded-glp-1s), [AJMC](https://www.ajmc.com/view/fda-panel-backs-6-peptides-for-compounding)

timeline.title: Spine-surgery meta-analysis finds GLP-1 drugs' effect on fusion healing depends on the operation, not the drug class
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis in European Spine Journal pooled twelve retrospective cohorts on GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure and outcomes after cervical spine fusion, and found signals pointing in opposite directions by procedure: anterior fusion estimates ranged from protective to neutral for pseudarthrosis (failed bone healing), while a semaglutide-specific posterior fusion cohort showed a roughly five-fold higher two-year pseudarthrosis signal. The authors stress the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating, with very high statistical heterogeneity, and call for procedure-specific validation rather than class-wide conclusions. Source: [Eur Spine J](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00586-026-10293-9)

timeline.title: Lilly-authored analysis reports tirzepatide cost offsets in older adults reached about 25% by 12-18 months — a number aimed at the Medicare Bridge debate
timeline.content: A matched cohort study in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, authored by Eli Lilly and collaborators using US claims data on 15,843 matched pairs of adults over 55 with obesity or overweight and no diabetes, reports that all-cause healthcare costs (excluding the drug) fell $319 per person per month more in tirzepatide users than in untreated controls by 12-18 months, driven by fewer hospital and emergency visits. The authors frame the offsets against the $195 monthly net Medicare cost under the Bridge programme — a live policy question as Medicare weighs obesity-drug coverage. As manufacturer-authored observational research on persistent users, the finding carries built-in selection caveats. Source: [Diabetes Obes Metab](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.71250)

timeline.title: Scoping review tallies the incretin-drugs-for-opioid-addiction literature: 21 studies, most of them in rodents
timeline.content: A scoping review in the Journal of Dual Diagnosis screened 857 papers on GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors in opioid use disorder and found 21 qualifying studies: thirteen preclinical (most showing reduced opioid-seeking behaviour in rodents), four observational analyses associating GLP-1 use with lower overdose rates, one preprint randomised trial, and three ongoing trials. The authors conclude the retrospective signals are promising but that ongoing controlled trials — including the NIH-network tirzepatide trial whose protocol published earlier this month — must read out before any treatment role is established. Source: [J Dual Diagn](https://doi.org/10.1080/15504263.2026.2720402)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 32 after the PCAC vote — the rulemaking clock, and why pharmacists say the counter has not changed
timeline.content: Thirty-two days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted at its 23-24 July 2026 meeting to recommend six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the regulatory file is still where it was: no proposed rule, no Federal Register notice, none of the six in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and no date or docket yet for the further PCAC meeting flagged for Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF. Today's angle is the clock rather than the vote. Legal and pharmacy commentary published since the meeting converges on the same sequence — removal from Category 2, then advisory recommendation, then Category 1 placement through notice-and-comment rulemaking — and on the same estimate, that the rulemaking step alone commonly runs eight to twelve months, so nothing changes at a dispensing counter in the meantime; one pharmacist-authored piece is titled precisely around that gap between headlines and practice. Analysts also note that FDA is reviewing the six recommendations and has made no decision, that the votes ran against the agency's own briefing document, and that committee reconstitution drew conflict-of-interest scrutiny. A separate and opposite track continues alongside it: FDA's April 2026 proposal to permanently exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list, and the agency's clarification that adding an ingredient such as vitamin B12 does not exempt a compounded GLP-1 from being treated as a copy of a commercially available drug. On the research side this period, the peptides in the compounding debate continue to generate mostly laboratory evidence — two new MOTS-c papers this week are a rat myocardial-infarction study and a review that calls the peptide "plausible but insufficiently validated" — while the approved incretin medicines generate large human datasets, including a 54,114-woman UK cohort reporting similar tirzepatide weight loss with and without self-reported PCOS and a review concluding that no baseline characteristic reliably predicts who responds. None of the six recommended peptides may lawfully be compounded today. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA PCAC meeting page](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/08/fda-advisory-committee-endorses-compounding-of-certain-peptides), [Pharmacy Times](https://www.pharmacytimes.com/view/what-the-peptide-vote-actually-changes-at-my-counter-hint-not-much-yet-), [AJMC](https://www.ajmc.com/view/fda-panel-backs-6-peptides-for-compounding), [J Endocr Soc](https://doi.org/10.1210/jendso/bvag177), [Bioact Mater](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bioactmat.2026.06.010)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 30 after the PCAC vote — the list still has not moved, and today the safety file grew on both sides of the approved/unapproved line
timeline.content: Thirty days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted at its 23–24 July 2026 meeting to recommend six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the regulatory record is unchanged: no proposed rule, no Federal Register notice, none of the six in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and no date or docket yet for the further PCAC meeting flagged for Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF. Legal commentary continues to stress that the votes are advisory, ran against FDA's own briefing, and require notice-and-comment rulemaking before anything may lawfully be compounded. Today's angle is safety, and it cuts both ways. On the approved side, a EudraVigilance disproportionality analysis published today reported eye-disorder and suicidal-ideation reporting signals for semaglutide and liraglutide relative to dulaglutide, while a meta-analysis pooling more than a million GLP-1 exposures found a roughly 40% higher rate of non-scarring hair loss that its authors attribute mainly to rapid weight loss rather than a direct drug effect — findings that sit alongside a separate meta-analysis reporting lower papilloedema and headache rates in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. On the unapproved side, the problems are pharmaceutical rather than pharmacological: the Partnership for Safe Medicines' August round-up records a nationwide voluntary recall of compounded injections from a Texas 503A pharmacy over elevated endotoxin levels, cease-and-desist and suspension actions by the California and Ohio boards of pharmacy against out-of-state mail-order compounders, arrests and peptide seizures in Malta, and Australian coverage of a death in a young man who had been using unregulated body-enhancement peptides. The through-line of the last month holds: the approved medicines generate large, messy datasets that regulators can weigh, while the compounding-list peptides generate paperwork and enforcement files. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — July 23–24, 2026 PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/08/fda-advisory-committee-endorses-compounding-of-certain-peptides), [Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol, DOI 10.1007/s00210-026-05813-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00210-026-05813-9), [Skin Appendage Disord, DOI 10.1159/000553070](https://doi.org/10.1159/000553070), [Partnership for Safe Medicines](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/08/august-10-2026.html)

timeline.title: European adverse-event database flags eye-disorder and suicidality reporting signals for semaglutide and liraglutide — the authors call it a signal, not a cause
timeline.content: A pharmacovigilance analysis published today in Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology examined suspected adverse reactions to semaglutide, liraglutide and dulaglutide reported to the European EudraVigilance database between 2020 and 2025. Eye disorders were reported disproportionately often with semaglutide compared with both liraglutide and dulaglutide, and suicidal ideation was reported disproportionately often with semaglutide and liraglutide compared with dulaglutide, though the confidence intervals on those suicidality estimates are very wide, reflecting small numbers. The authors note that regulators have not established a causal link for suicidality and conclude that the possibility should not be underestimated and merits further study. Disproportionality analyses of voluntary reports measure reporting patterns, not incidence, and cannot establish causation. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol, DOI 10.1007/s00210-026-05813-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00210-026-05813-9) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Meta-analysis of more than a million GLP-1 exposures reports about 40% more non-scarring hair loss — and points at the weight loss, not the drug
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis in Skin Appendage Disorders pooled 17 studies covering 1,091,743 patient-exposures and found a pooled odds ratio of 1.40 for any non-scarring alopecia among GLP-1 receptor agonist users, with the signal driven by telogen effluvium and androgenetic alopecia at 12 months. Alopecia areata was not significantly associated, and a subgroup with central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia was mostly recorded as improving. The authors' stated interpretation is that the effect is mediated primarily by micronutrient deficiency accompanying rapid weight loss rather than by a direct action of the drug on the hair follicle — a mechanism that would apply to fast weight loss from any cause. The analysis combines cohort data with spontaneous-report signals, which limits how far causation can be read into it. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Skin Appendage Disord, DOI 10.1159/000553070](https://doi.org/10.1159/000553070) (PubMed)

timeline.title: A rarer condition gets a GLP-1 readout: pooled data in idiopathic intracranial hypertension show less papilloedema and headache, on low-certainty evidence
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis in Headache pooled eight studies covering 13,243 patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension — raised pressure around the brain, a condition strongly linked to obesity — and reported that GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with roughly half the risk of papilloedema at three months, sustained at 24 months, along with lower headache frequency, fewer visual disturbances and less refractory disease. The authors qualify the result heavily: the evidence base is dominated by observational studies at moderate to serious risk of confounding, the certainty is low, and the pooled numbers are meant to justify and shape randomised trials rather than to guide practice. No GLP-1 medicine is approved for this indication. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Headache, DOI 10.1111/head.70131](https://doi.org/10.1111/head.70131) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Compounding's other file: an endotoxin recall, two state boards moving against unlicensed mail-order pharmacies, and seizures abroad
timeline.content: While the 503A listing question sits with FDA, the compounded-peptide supply chain has generated a separate record of enforcement, collected in the Partnership for Safe Medicines' August round-up. A licensed 503A compounding pharmacy in Austin, Texas issued a voluntary nationwide recall of three lots of compounded injections after elevated endotoxin levels were found, with FDA noting reports of nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and injection-site reactions and warning that anaphylactic shock and death are associated with high endotoxin in injectables. Separately, the California Board of Pharmacy issued a cease-and-desist to a Texas compounder said to have shipped more than 250,000 prescriptions into the state without a licence, and the Ohio Board of Pharmacy summarily suspended another Texas mail-order pharmacy over thousands of unlicensed shipments. Internationally, four people were arrested in Malta after officers seized more than 2,000 units of peptides and steroids, and Australian outlets reported the death of a 33-year-old man who had used unregulated body-enhancement peptides, alongside University of Queensland findings that sampled products were under-dosed, over-dosed or contained no active ingredient. These are quality, licensure and provenance failures rather than findings about any peptide's biology. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Partnership for Safe Medicines](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/08/august-10-2026.html), [FDA — recalls and safety alerts](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts)

timeline.title: Fourteen years of US prescribing data: GLP-1 initiations up more than twentyfold, and about half of patients still on treatment at one year
timeline.content: A cohort study in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice used Optum Labs claims and electronic health records to track 342,932 treatment initiations among US adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity from 2010 to 2024. GLP-1 receptor agonists made up 60.8% of initiations and rose from 1,988 annual starts to 44,852, dwarfing metabolic and bariatric surgery, which stayed rare. Semaglutide and tirzepatide together accounted for almost 95% of GLP-1 starts in 2024. The durability numbers are the more striking part: median GLP-1 treatment duration was 240 days, about half of initiators met the adherence threshold, and 53.0% were still on their starting therapy at one year, with tirzepatide performing best on both measures. The sample covers privately insured and Medicare Advantage enrollees, so cash-pay and uninsured patterns are not captured. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Diabetes Res Clin Pract, DOI 10.1016/j.diabres.2026.113504](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2026.113504) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Three trials registered this week take on the muscle-loss question, alcohol craving, and adolescent metabolic health
timeline.content: New ClinicalTrials.gov entries show researchers moving on questions the current evidence leaves unresolved. The Technical University of Munich registered a Phase 4 randomised trial (NCT07777575) putting 150 adults with obesity on tirzepatide with or without supervised resistance training and measuring thigh muscle volume — a direct test of whether exercise offsets the lean-mass loss that has shadowed this drug class. Yale University registered a Phase 1 study (NCT07772960) in 90 participants with alcohol use disorder and obesity, comparing two semaglutide dose levels against placebo on craving, alcohol use and stress-hormone measures. Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center registered a Phase 4 study (NCT07770152) of semaglutide plus lifestyle counselling in 42 young people with autism spectrum disorder and obesity. None has results, and none of these uses is an approved indication. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07777575](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07777575), [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07772960](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07772960), [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07770152](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07770152)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 29 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file has not moved, and today's new evidence is all about what GLP-1 drugs do to the brain
timeline.content: Twenty-nine days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, nothing in the regulatory record has changed: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six is in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and the further PCAC meeting flagged for Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF still has no date or docket. The legal analyses published since the vote continue to say the same two things — the recommendations are advisory and ran against FDA's own briefing, and notice-and-comment rulemaking is measured in quarters or years — so none of the six may lawfully be compounded today. Today's angle is neurological. Two papers on GLP-1 receptor agonists and the brain surfaced within a day of each other and point in opposite directions. A retrospective cohort in BMJ Mental Health followed 13,007 adults with psychiatric diagnoses and reported that those who started semaglutide had fewer clinician-recorded cognitive signs and symptoms over 12 months than comparison groups, with the signal strongest for memory and consistently significant only in major depression — and the authors say outright that randomised trials are needed before causality can be claimed. On the same days, a Bradford Hill-informed systematic evaluation in Current Psychiatry Reports worked through the reported neuropsychiatric associations of this drug class — depression, anxiety, suicidality, reward behaviour, cognition, ocular effects — and concluded that biological plausibility exists but the evidence remains insufficient to establish causality for most outcomes. That tension is now being taken into trials: two Phase 3 semaglutide studies were registered on ClinicalTrials.gov in the past week, one of them a 600-participant randomised trial in people with schizophrenia and metabolic syndrome. The pattern of the last month holds — the approved GLP-1 medicines keep generating large-scale data with real uncertainty inside it, while the compounding-list peptides generate paperwork. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney](https://www.bipc.com/fda-pcac-recommends-six-peptides-for-the-503a-bulks-list-what-compounding-pharmacies-need-to-know), [BMJ Ment Health, DOI 10.1136/bmjment-2026-302828](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2026-302828), [Curr Psychiatry Rep, DOI 10.1007/s11920-026-01709-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-026-01709-w), [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07770282](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07770282)

timeline.title: Two papers on GLP-1 drugs and the brain land together — one finds a cognition signal, the other says causality is not established
timeline.content: A retrospective cohort study in BMJ Mental Health used de-identified US electronic health records to follow 13,007 adults with a psychiatric diagnosis who had clinician-rated cognitive assessments before and after starting an antidiabetic drug, 1,261 of whom started semaglutide. Over 12 months the semaglutide group had a lower composite score of recorded cognitive signs and symptoms than those on no antidiabetic treatment, glipizide or empagliflozin, with the effect strongest for memory and consistently significant only in major depression; the authors call for randomised trials before drawing conclusions. Published alongside it, a Bradford Hill-informed systematic evaluation in Current Psychiatry Reports assessed the reported links between GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists and a range of neuropsychiatric outcomes, and concluded that while a biological relationship is plausible, current evidence is insufficient to establish causality for most of them. Read together the two describe an open question, not a settled one. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [BMJ Ment Health, DOI 10.1136/bmjment-2026-302828](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2026-302828), [Curr Psychiatry Rep, DOI 10.1007/s11920-026-01709-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-026-01709-w) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Matched cohort reports much higher ulcerative colitis remission rates among patients on GLP-1 drugs — and weight loss did not explain it
timeline.content: A retrospective study in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases matched 150 adults with ulcerative colitis who started semaglutide or liraglutide for metabolic reasons against 150 comparable patients who did not, using records from a single academic health system covering 2022–2024. Symptomatic remission was recorded far more often in the GLP-1 group at 12 weeks (66.7% versus 25.3%), the association survived multivariable adjustment, and an endoscopic subset showed higher endoscopic remission too. The detail the authors highlight is that weight loss was not associated with remission, which points away from the simplest explanation. It remains a single-centre retrospective analysis of patients treated for a different indication, and neither drug is FDA approved for ulcerative colitis; the paper frames the result as grounds for randomised testing of an adjunctive role. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Inflamm Bowel Dis, DOI 10.1093/ibd/izag167](https://doi.org/10.1093/ibd/izag167) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two new Phase 3 semaglutide trials appear on the registry — a once-daily oral formulation in obesity, and a cardiometabolic study in schizophrenia
timeline.content: ClinicalTrials.gov records show two Phase 3 semaglutide studies posted in the past week. The first (NCT07770841), sponsored by Novo Nordisk, is a randomised placebo-controlled trial of once-daily oral semaglutide in 450 adults with overweight or obesity across 62 sites, which began recruiting on 12 August 2026 with primary completion scheduled for February 2028. The second (NCT07770282), the ESCaMS trial run by the All India Institute of Medical Sciences Bhubaneswar, is a 600-participant multicentre double-blind randomised trial of semaglutide versus placebo added to usual care, testing the cardiometabolic profile of people with schizophrenia and metabolic syndrome — a population in which antipsychotic-associated weight gain and cardiovascular risk are long-standing problems. It is listed as not yet recruiting, with a December 2026 start and primary completion in 2030. Registration is not evidence of benefit; both are years from a readout. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07770841](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07770841), [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07770282](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07770282)

timeline.title: Clinic case series reports muscle mass and grip strength rising during tirzepatide weight loss — but the design cannot say what caused it
timeline.content: Loss of lean mass during incretin-based weight loss is one of the more persistent concerns about this drug class, and a retrospective case series in Obesity Pillars offers a data point on it. Ninety-three men with obesity and symptomatic testosterone deficiency at a single outpatient clinic received weekly tirzepatide alongside testosterone therapy and coaching focused on resistance exercise and protein intake. Over 12 months bodyweight fell about 18–20% and fat mass 38–40%; lean body mass declined, but bioimpedance-estimated skeletal muscle mass rose about 4–12% and grip strength about 18–21%, with improvements in HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, hs-CRP and patient-reported health scores. The authors state clearly that the uncontrolled multimodal design means no individual component can be credited, and bioimpedance estimates muscle rather than measuring it. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Obes Pillars, DOI 10.1016/j.obpill.2026.100317](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obpill.2026.100317) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 28 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file is unchanged, and the peptide with the most new evidence today is one queued for the NEXT review, not this one
timeline.content: Twenty-eight days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the agency's position is where it has been all month: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six appears in the final list at 21 CFR 216.23, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed without a date or docket. Law-firm and policy analyses continue to make the same two points — the votes are advisory and ran against FDA's own briefing recommendation, and notice-and-comment rulemaking can take well over a year — so none of the six may lawfully be compounded today. Today's angle is a quieter one: the peptide that gained the most published evidence this week is not on the recommended list at all but in the queue behind it. GHK-Cu, one of the substances awaiting the next PCAC review, received what appears to be its first systematic review in a peer-reviewed surgical journal, and the tally is instructive — 20 studies met inclusion criteria, of which 18 were preclinical and only 2 were randomised controlled trials, with the authors concluding the biological rationale is reasonable but the clinical evidence base is too thin and too methodologically varied to support standardised practice. That ratio is a fair summary of where most of the compounding-debate peptides sit. Meanwhile the approved GLP-1 medicines continue to generate large-scale clinical data: a prespecified secondary analysis of the 17,604-patient SELECT trial published in Circulation reported that semaglutide cut the inflammatory marker hsCRP by about 38%, with the fall appearing within weeks and occurring even in participants who did not lose weight, and a propensity-matched real-world comparison in Obesity found no difference between tirzepatide and injectable semaglutide in serious liver outcomes. Both are covered separately below. The contrast is the story: one group of molecules is being characterised in trials of tens of thousands of people, the other is still being argued about on the strength of animal work. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/08/fda-advisory-committee-endorses-compounding-of-certain-peptides), [Aesthet Surg J, DOI 10.1093/asj/sjag169](https://doi.org/10.1093/asj/sjag169), [Circulation, DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.074482](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.074482), [Obesity, DOI 10.1002/oby.70277](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.70277)

timeline.title: GHK-Cu gets its first systematic review — and the count is 18 preclinical studies to 2 randomised trials
timeline.content: A PRISMA-guided systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal searched three databases from inception through March 2026 for studies of the copper peptide GHK-Cu used on its own in aesthetic medicine, and found 20 eligible studies: 18 preclinical and 2 randomised controlled trials. Laboratory and animal work consistently reported increased extracellular matrix synthesis, modulation of metalloproteinase activity, promotion of angiogenesis and cell proliferation, and anti-inflammatory effects via suppression of TGF-beta and IL-6, while microneedle and liposomal delivery improved transdermal bioavailability. The two clinical trials reported better patient-reported satisfaction after laser resurfacing and reduced wrinkle volume and depth against controls. The authors' own conclusion is the important part: the biological rationale is reasonable, but methodological variability and the small number of well-designed clinical trials mean larger controlled trials with standardised formulations and delivery methods are needed before consistent clinical practice can be built on it. GHK-Cu is sold in the US as a cosmetic ingredient, is not an FDA-approved drug, and is one of the substances queued for the FDA advisory committee's next 503A compounding review. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Aesthet Surg J, DOI 10.1093/asj/sjag169](https://doi.org/10.1093/asj/sjag169) (PubMed)

timeline.title: SELECT substudy in Circulation: semaglutide cut an inflammatory marker by about a third, and the drop started before the weight loss did
timeline.content: A prespecified secondary analysis of the SELECT trial, published in Circulation, looked at high-sensitivity C-reactive protein across all 17,604 participants with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity but without diabetes. Baseline hsCRP predicted risk — major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death and all-cause death all rose across increasing hsCRP bands — and semaglutide lowered hsCRP by 37.8% at 104 weeks while reducing event risk across every band. Notably, the reduction was visible by weeks 4 and 8, before substantial weight loss, and was also seen in participants who lost no weight, and it was independent of LDL cholesterol, statin use and how patients qualified for the trial. The authors present reduced inflammation as contributing in part to semaglutide's cardiovascular benefit, while treating hsCRP as a prognostic biomarker rather than a demonstrated mechanism. This is a secondary analysis of one trial in a specific population. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Circulation, DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.074482](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.074482) (PubMed), [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03574597](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03574597)

timeline.title: Two liver files: tirzepatide and semaglutide look equivalent on serious liver outcomes, while a Japanese switching cohort reports fibrosis-index gains
timeline.content: A retrospective target trial emulation in Obesity used the TriNetX global network to match new users of tirzepatide against new users of injectable semaglutide among adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, and over a median of about 17 months found no significant difference in a composite of cirrhosis, decompensated events and hepatocellular carcinoma (4.05 versus 4.04 per 1000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.88–1.23), holding across a MASLD subgroup and an as-treated analysis; tirzepatide produced a greater BMI reduction of roughly 1.1 kg/m2. Separately, a multicentre Japanese secondary analysis in the Journal of Diabetes and its Complications followed 182 patients at high risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease who switched from a GLP-1 receptor agonist to tirzepatide, and reported falls in HbA1c, bodyweight and liver enzymes over six months, with a significant improvement in the FIB-4 fibrosis index confined to the high-fibrosis-risk group and not explained by changes in bodyweight or HbA1c. Both studies are retrospective and non-randomised, rely on database codes or surrogate hepatic indices rather than biopsy, and cover a relatively short follow-up. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Obesity, DOI 10.1002/oby.70277](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.70277), [J Diabetes Complications, DOI 10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2026.109391](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2026.109391) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 27 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file is unchanged, and the week's sharpest signal is an eye-safety meta-analysis on semaglutide
timeline.content: Twenty-seven days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the agency's position is where it was: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six appears in 21 CFR 216.23, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as before the end of February 2027, without a date or docket. Worth restating from the record: FDA's own briefing materials for the July meeting had proposed against inclusion, including for TB-500 acetate, so the recommendations run against the agency's staff position, and none of the six may lawfully be compounded today. Today's angle is safety surveillance rather than the compounding file. A new meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Pharmacology pooled eight cohort studies covering 5.9 million people and reported a roughly two-fold relative risk of non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy among semaglutide users, with very high heterogeneity and no randomised data — a finding that sits alongside an unusually uneven international regulatory picture, in which the World Health Organization and the European Medicines Agency already treat NAION as a very rare labelled adverse effect of semaglutide while it is not listed in the US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy or Rybelsus. Two further clinical syntheses landed the same week on the benefit side — a five-trial meta-analysis in obstructive sleep apnoea and a small prospective cohort on sleep and mood — and on the research-peptide side, an eLife paper redescribed MOTS-c, one of the six recommended substances, as a mitochondrial-encoded antimicrobial peptide in cells and mice. All are covered separately below. The pattern for the recovery peptides is unchanged: the human evidence remains absent while the regulatory question stays open. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — July 23-24, 2026 PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [FDA — PCAC briefing document](https://www.fda.gov/media/193342/download), [Federal Register — PCAC notice, 16 Apr 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/16/2026-07361/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-notice-of-meeting-establishment-of-a-public-docket-request), [J Clin Pharmacol, DOI 10.1002/jcph.70248](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.70248), [EMA — semaglutide NAION review](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/referrals/semaglutide), [eLife, DOI 10.7554/eLife.87615](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87615)

timeline.title: Pooled analysis of 5.9 million patients reports a two-fold relative risk of a rare optic-nerve condition on semaglutide — with the caveats doing a lot of work
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Pharmacology combined eight observational cohort studies covering 5,916,559 participants, 1,870,346 of them semaglutide-treated, and found a higher relative risk of non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy — an abrupt, usually permanent loss of vision in one eye — at a relative effect of 1.93 (95% CI 1.22 to 3.08). The signal was statistically significant in the diabetes subgroup but not among people who were overweight or obese without diabetes, and heterogeneity across the pooled studies was very high. The authors are explicit that all the included evidence is observational and that randomised trials are needed to settle causality; the absolute risk described in the wider literature is low. The regulatory picture is uneven: the European Medicines Agency and the World Health Organization already recognise NAION as a very rare adverse effect of semaglutide, while it is not currently listed in the US prescribing information. Anyone taking one of these medicines who develops sudden vision changes should contact a clinician; this is general research, not medical advice. Source: [J Clin Pharmacol, DOI 10.1002/jcph.70248](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcph.70248) (PubMed), [WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/27-06-2025-27-06-2025-semaglutide-medicines-naion)

timeline.title: Two clinical syntheses on the benefit side: a five-trial meta-analysis in sleep apnoea, and a small prospective cohort on sleep quality and mood
timeline.content: In Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, a PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis screened 3,836 articles and pooled five randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists — liraglutide and tirzepatide — in obstructive sleep apnoea, covering 948 patients. The pooled reduction in the apnoea–hypopnoea index was 12.4 events per hour more than control (95% CI −17.2 to −7.7), reported as independent of whether patients were using continuous positive airway pressure, alongside greater weight loss, smaller waist circumference and modest blood-pressure reductions; gastrointestinal adverse events were more common on treatment. Separately, in the Journal of Endocrinological Investigation, a prospective cohort of 78 adults with obesity starting semaglutide or tirzepatide recorded falls in depressive-symptom and sleep-quality scores at three months, with baseline severity — not weight loss or drug choice — predicting response. The sleep-apnoea synthesis rests on only five trials; the sleep-and-mood cohort is small, uncontrolled and unblinded. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg, DOI 10.1002/ohn.70407](https://doi.org/10.1002/ohn.70407), [J Endocrinol Invest, DOI 10.1007/s40618-026-03024-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40618-026-03024-w) (PubMed)

timeline.title: MOTS-c, one of the six peptides the FDA panel recommended, is redescribed in eLife as a mitochondrial-encoded antimicrobial peptide
timeline.content: Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology report in eLife that MOTS-c — a microprotein encoded inside the human mitochondrial genome rather than the nuclear one — has the chemistry and behaviour of a host defense peptide. In laboratory assays it acted against Escherichia coli and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by disrupting bacterial membranes, and in a mouse peritonitis model it neutralised MRSA infectivity; in human monocytes, immune signals induced the cell's own MOTS-c, and adding the peptide during mouse monocyte differentiation produced macrophages with interferon- and antigen-presentation-related signatures and better bacterial clearance. The authors present it as the first mitochondrial-encoded host defense peptide, arguing innate immunity is partly written in mitochondrial DNA. Separately in Experimental Neurology, a mouse traumatic-brain-injury proteomics study reported that SS-31 partially mitigated selected redox and white-matter abnormalities. Both are cell and animal studies with no human treatment data; MOTS-c is not an approved drug, and SS-31 (elamipretide) is FDA-approved only for Barth syndrome. Source: [eLife, DOI 10.7554/eLife.87615](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87615), [Exp Neurol, DOI 10.1016/j.expneurol.2026.115979](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.expneurol.2026.115979) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 26 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file is still frozen while the centre of gravity in the field shifts to oral, non-peptide drugs
timeline.content: Twenty-six days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the agency's position is unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six appears in 21 CFR 216.23, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF remains listed only as before the end of February 2027, without a date or docket. Law-firm and policy analyses continue to stress the same points — the votes are advisory, they overrode FDA's own briefing recommendation, and none of the six may lawfully be compounded today. Today's angle is what the recommendation is competing against. The best-resourced part of this field is no longer peptide at all: Lilly's once-daily orforglipron, approved as Foundayo on 1 April 2026, is a small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, and its 52-week Japanese Phase 3 safety results published this week in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. Trade coverage of the oral market describes Novo's Wegovy pill plateauing near a third of its franchise's prescriptions while Foundayo reported $98 million in second-quarter sales. Alongside that, this week's publications ran to a CagriSema meta-analysis of seven trials, a retatrutide biomarker post hoc, an expert consensus on incretin use in neuroendocrine tumours, and — for the recovery peptides — two preclinical papers on thymosin beta-4 in colitis and on LL-37 in melanoma, all covered separately below. The pattern is consistent: the approved, commercially serious weight-management options are moving toward orally available small molecules, while the peptides in the compounding debate remain at the animal-study stage. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — July 23-24, 2026 PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney](https://www.bipc.com/fda-pcac-recommends-six-peptides-for-the-503a-bulks-list-what-compounding-pharmacies-need-to-know), [Health Affairs Forefront](https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/fda-advisory-committee-s-vote-may-open-drug-compounding-back-door-unapproved-peptides), [Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00138-5](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00138-5), [Fierce Pharma](https://www.fiercepharma.com/pharma/oral-glp-1-tracker-launch-trajectories-lilly-foundayo-novo-wegovy-pill)

timeline.title: Phase 3 safety data for the oral GLP-1 orforglipron publish as the oral weight-loss market splits between two pills
timeline.content: ACHIEVE-J, a 401-participant open-label Phase 3 trial across 40 Japanese centres published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, assessed 52-week safety of once-daily oral orforglipron added to diet and exercise or to one or two oral antidiabetic medicines in adults with type 2 diabetes. Eighty-five percent of participants had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event, mostly mild or moderate; discontinuation for adverse events rose with dose from 5% to 14%, gastrointestinal symptoms were the most common cause, and no severe hypoglycaemia occurred. The trial was manufacturer-funded and open-label. Commercially, orforglipron was approved by the FDA as Foundayo on 1 April 2026 and trade coverage reports it generated $98 million in second-quarter sales while Novo's Wegovy pill has hovered near a third of total Wegovy prescriptions. Orforglipron is a small molecule, not a peptide, and is tracked here for context. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00138-5](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00138-5) (PubMed), [Eli Lilly](https://investor.lilly.com/news-releases/news-release-details/fda-approves-lillys-foundayotm-orforglipron-only-glp-1-pill), [Fierce Pharma](https://www.fiercepharma.com/pharma/oral-glp-1-tracker-launch-trajectories-lilly-foundayo-novo-wegovy-pill)

timeline.title: Two investigational-pipeline readouts: a seven-trial CagriSema meta-analysis and a retatrutide biomarker post hoc
timeline.content: A GRADE-assessed systematic review in Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology pooled seven randomised trials covering 8,069 adults with overweight or obesity and found the fixed-dose cagrilintide/semaglutide combination produced greater weight reduction than semaglutide alone (mean difference −7.58 kg), cagrilintide alone (−9.24 kg) or placebo (−13.99 kg), with adverse events mainly gastrointestinal and injection-site related and no excess of serious events. Separately, a manufacturer-authored post hoc analysis in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism of two Phase 2 retatrutide trials reported placebo-adjusted reductions in non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particles in both studies, and in C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 in the obesity-without-diabetes study. Both are investigational agents; neither is approved, and biomarker changes are not cardiovascular outcomes. Source: [Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol, DOI 10.1007/s00210-026-05809-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00210-026-05809-5), [Diabetes Obes Metab, DOI 10.1111/dom.71200](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.71200) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Recovery-peptide research this week is preclinical: thymosin beta-4 in experimental colitis, and LL-37 in melanoma-skin crosstalk
timeline.content: Two laboratory papers touched peptides that sit in the FDA compounding debate. In Molecular Biomedicine, researchers found the thymosin beta-4 gene downregulated in colonic tissue from inflammatory bowel disease patients, showed that mice lacking it were more susceptible to chemically induced colitis, and reported that oral recombinant human thymosin beta-4 improved survival and reduced epithelial injury and fibrosis markers in mouse colitis models, apparently via suppression of mineralocorticoid receptor signalling. In Cell Reports, a separate group reported that melanoma-derived exosomes suppress the cathelicidin peptide LL-37 in neighbouring keratinocytes through a microRNA acting on EGFR signalling, and that keratinocyte LL-37 restrained melanoma migration and growth in mice. Both are animal and cell studies with no human treatment data; TB-500 is a related fragment rather than full-length thymosin beta-4, and LL-37 is one of five substances queued for the next PCAC review. Source: [Mol Biomed, DOI 10.1186/s43556-026-00539-9](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43556-026-00539-9), [Cell Rep, DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2026.117837](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.117837) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two special-population files on GLP-1 drugs: an expert consensus in neuroendocrine tumours and an orthopaedic cohort in ankle osteoarthritis
timeline.content: An expert consensus statement published August 15 in Cancer addresses a question clinicians have been raising as incretin use widens — whether GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin agonists are safe in people with neuroendocrine neoplasms. The authors note that some preclinical receptor-expressing models show tumour growth with GLP-1 receptor activation, that receptor expression varies widely and is often absent in common ileal tumours, and that retrospective clinical data have not shown a consistent oncological risk increase, while calling for individualised assessment and surveillance pending prospective data. Separately, a TriNetX cohort study in Foot & Ankle Specialist reported that among adults with obesity, GLP-1 users had lower rates of ankle joint injection and ankle arthroplasty or arthrodesis, whereas among adults with type 2 diabetes they had a higher rate of ankle arthroscopy — a mixed picture the authors say shows metabolic improvement does not translate uniformly into musculoskeletal benefit. Source: [Cancer, DOI 10.1002/cncr.70586](https://doi.org/10.1002/cncr.70586), [Foot Ankle Spec, DOI 10.1177/19386400261471652](https://doi.org/10.1177/19386400261471652) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 25 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file is still frozen, and all the movement has shifted into the development pipeline
timeline.content: Twenty-five days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, nothing has changed on the agency's side: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, none of the six has been added to the final 503A list, no interim enforcement policy has been announced, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF remains listed only as before the end of February 2027, with no date or docket. Law-firm analyses continue to make the same two points — that the votes are non-binding, and that notice-and-comment rulemaking can run well over a year — so the practical position is unchanged: none of the six may lawfully be compounded today. The separate 503B question is also still open, with the FDA's April 2026 proposal to exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the outsourcing-facility bulks list sitting in post-comment review. With both compounding tracks stalled, this week's actual news is developmental rather than regulatory, and it is notably not about the recovery peptides at all. Three of the week's publications point the GLP-1 field outward: a Chinese phase 2 trial of an oral nonpeptide GLP-1 receptor agonist reported double-digit weight reduction over 16 weeks, an NIH clinical-trials-network group published the protocol for the first randomised test of tirzepatide in opioid use disorder, and a 32-trial meta-analysis pulled apart how differently tirzepatide and semaglutide behave on blood pressure. A Japanese randomised trial adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to semaglutide in biopsy-proven MASH missed its primary histology endpoints. All four are covered separately below. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/08/fda-advisory-committee-endorses-compounding-of-certain-peptides), [FDA — 503B proposal](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-proposes-exclude-semaglutide-tirzepatide-and-liraglutide-503b-bulks-list), [Signal Transduct Target Ther, DOI 10.1038/s41392-026-02859-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41392-026-02859-2), [Endocrine, DOI 10.1007/s12020-026-04757-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12020-026-04757-7)

timeline.title: Adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to semaglutide did not significantly improve liver histology in a 52-week MASH trial
timeline.content: A Japanese open-label randomised trial published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism gave 60 adults with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and type 2 diabetes either semaglutide plus luseogliflozin or semaglutide alone at antidiabetic doses, with paired biopsies at baseline and week 52 read by blinded pathologists. Every histological endpoint numerically favoured the combination — MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis in 34.9% versus 19.4%, and fibrosis improvement in 26.9% versus 13.9% — but none reached significance in the pre-specified primary analysis, and only the NAFLD activity score improvement was nominally significant in the per-protocol set. The combination did produce greater falls in bodyweight, HbA1c, aminotransferases and liver stiffness, with no new safety concerns. The trial was small, open-label, and had unequal arms. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Diabetes Obes Metab, DOI 10.1111/dom.71233](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.71233) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Meta-analysis of 32 randomised trials finds tirzepatide and semaglutide behave differently on blood pressure
timeline.content: Pooling 32 randomised controlled trials covering 47,332 participants treated for type 2 diabetes or obesity, a systematic review in Endocrine reports that tirzepatide was associated with markedly fewer hypertension-related adverse events (risk ratio 0.40) but roughly two-and-a-half times the rate of hypotension-related events, with the hypotension signal larger in higher-dose subgroups. Semaglutide showed no significant association in either direction. The authors present the contrast as a reason to weigh baseline blood pressure and cardiometabolic risk when choosing between the two agents rather than as evidence of harm. Source: [Endocrine, DOI 10.1007/s12020-026-04757-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12020-026-04757-7) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two pipeline signals: the first randomised trial of tirzepatide in opioid use disorder, and phase 2 results for an oral nonpeptide GLP-1 agonist
timeline.content: Investigators with the NIH National Drug Abuse Treatment Clinical Trials Network published the design of TAB in Contemporary Clinical Trials — a nine-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomising about 310 adults with moderate-to-severe opioid use disorder who recently started buprenorphine to tirzepatide or placebo, with six-month treatment retention as the primary outcome. It is the first randomised test of tirzepatide in this indication, and the paper reports protocol only, no results. Separately, in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, a 250-participant phase 2 trial in China of VCT220 — an orally available nonpeptide GLP-1 receptor agonist, a small molecule rather than a peptide — reported mean weight reductions of 5.75% to 9.73% over 16 weeks versus 1.61% on placebo, with mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal adverse events during titration. VCT220 is investigational and not approved anywhere; its sponsor has authors on the paper. Source: [Contemp Clin Trials, DOI 10.1016/j.cct.2026.108437](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cct.2026.108437), [Signal Transduct Target Ther, DOI 10.1038/s41392-026-02859-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41392-026-02859-2) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 22 after the PCAC vote — the US compounding file is still frozen while Canada moves the opposite way on the same molecules
timeline.content: Twenty-two days after the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the agency's own pages remain unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as "before the end of February 2027," with no date or docket. Today's angle is the contrast across the border. While the US process points, however slowly, toward a possible compounding pathway, Canada has been tightening: Health Canada's standing public advisory warns against buying or injecting unauthorised peptide drugs sold online — naming products including BPC-157, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, TB-500 and retatrutide — and in June 2026 the Superior Court of Québec granted the regulator a permanent injunction against a retailer selling unauthorised injectable peptides. A CBC News investigation published in early August then reported that some Canadian physicians are nonetheless routing patients to an unauthorised peptide through a compounding gap, drawing criticism from academic commentators (covered separately below). Two peptides sit on both lists at once, which is a reminder that a favourable advisory vote in one jurisdiction is not a safety finding and carries no weight in another. On the research side the week's publications were squarely metabolic: a Novo Nordisk phase 3b trial of a once-weekly insulin-plus-semaglutide combination, a post hoc count of combined risk-factor targets across the tirzepatide SURMOUNT programme, and a systematic review assembling the small published gastroparesis case literature (all below). This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [Health Canada public advisory](https://recalls-rappels.canada.ca/en/alert-recall/think-twice-injecting-peptides-bought-online-unauthorized-products-can-seriously-harm), [Health Canada — permanent injunction](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/news/2026/07/health-canada-obtains-permanent-injunction-preventing-canlab-researchs-illegal-sale-of-injectable-peptides-in-canada.html), [CBC News](https://www.cbc.ca/news/investigates/unauthorized-peptide-loophole-bpc157-9.7281300), [Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00136-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00136-1)

timeline.title: Novo Nordisk phase 3b trial puts a once-weekly insulin-plus-semaglutide combination against daily basal insulin
timeline.content: COMBINE 4, published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, randomised 485 insulin-naive adults with type 2 diabetes across 97 sites in nine countries to once-weekly IcoSema — a fixed combination of basal insulin icodec and semaglutide — or to once-daily insulin glargine U100, over 40 weeks. HbA1c fell further on the combination (−3.32 vs −2.44 percentage points), mean bodyweight decreased on IcoSema while increasing on glargine (−0.79 vs +3.81 kg), and rates of clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia were lower with the combination; gastrointestinal effects were its most common adverse events. The trial was funded by Novo Nordisk with company-affiliated authors, and IcoSema is investigational rather than approved. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00136-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00136-1) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two PLOS ONE papers: a tirzepatide risk-factor tally across SURMOUNT, and the first systematic sweep of GLP-1 gastroparesis case reports
timeline.content: A manufacturer-authored post hoc analysis pooled SURMOUNT-1 through SURMOUNT-4 and counted participants meeting a combined target of weight reduction, a systolic blood-pressure fall of at least 5 mmHg and non-HDL cholesterol below 130 mg/dL: 32–38% on tirzepatide versus 2–8% on placebo at the 5% weight threshold, and 22–34% versus 1–3% at the 15% threshold. Separately, a PRISMA-guided systematic review searching four databases through October 2025 found only twelve published case reports of GLP-1-associated gastroparesis covering thirteen patients — semaglutide most often implicated, onset frequently after dose escalation or restarting, and symptoms resolving in every case once the drug was stopped — with the authors emphasising that a case literature this small cannot establish incidence. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [PLoS One, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0345032](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345032), [PLoS One, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0354497](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354497) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: three weeks after the PCAC vote the compounding file is still silent — and the scrutiny has shifted to the GLP-1 safety ledger on both sides of the Atlantic
timeline.content: Twenty-one days after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, FDA's own pages remain unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as "before the end of February 2027." With the regulatory file quiet, this week's story is safety accounting. A BMJ news feature published August 12 tallies the UK regulator MHRA's Yellow Card data on GLP-1 medicines — hundreds of thousands of adverse-event reports and about 216 reports with a fatal outcome — while stressing that such reports record suspicion, not confirmed causation, and quoting the MHRA's reassurance that the medicines are safe for the majority of users. The same day, an Anesthesiology analysis pushed in the other direction on a long-running safety question: in matched surgical patients, preoperative GLP-1 use was associated with lower short-term postoperative mortality and no added aspiration risk (covered below, alongside a new liver-cancer analysis). General research only — not medical advice. timeline.title: BMJ examines the UK regulator's tally of deaths reported in association with GLP-1 drugs — and what those reports do and don't mean
timeline.content: A BMJ news feature reviews the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency's Yellow Card pharmacovigilance data for GLP-1 medicines: roughly 106,000 adverse-reaction reports for tirzepatide (120 with fatal outcome), about 48,000 for semaglutide as Wegovy (59 deaths) and about 4,500 for liraglutide as Saxenda (37 deaths). The piece emphasises that a Yellow Card report reflects a reporter's suspicion rather than confirmed causation — underlying illness can account for many outcomes — and quotes the MHRA reassuring patients that GLP-1 medicines are safe for the majority of users while surveillance continues. Source: [BMJ, DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100557](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100557)

timeline.title: Two real-world files: lower postoperative mortality with preoperative GLP-1 use, and lower five-year liver-cancer risk in GLP-1 initiators
timeline.content: In Anesthesiology, a TriNetX propensity-matched analysis of adult surgical patients with type 2 diabetes (2013–2023) reported that preoperative GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with lower 14-day postoperative mortality versus metformin (0.98% vs 2.20%) and versus DPP-4 inhibitors, with less bacterial pneumonia and no increase in aspiration pneumonitis against any comparator — observational findings the authors say need prospective confirmation. In Hepatology International, a target-trial emulation using UT Southwestern PCORnet data linked GLP-1 initiation to a lower five-year risk of hepatocellular carcinoma versus metformin, insulin, DPP-4 inhibitors and sulfonylureas. Source: [Anesthesiology, DOI 10.1097/ALN.0000000000006326](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000006326), [Hepatol Int, DOI 10.1007/s12072-026-11138-9](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12072-026-11138-9) (PubMed)

timeline.title: GHK-Cu — copper peptide provides the oxygen-generating step in a preclinical diabetic-wound dressing
timeline.content: Researchers in Carbohydrate Polymers describe an injectable hydrogel for diabetic wounds in which glucose oxidase consumes excess wound glucose and produces hydrogen peroxide, and GHK-Cu then converts that peroxide to oxygen — pairing antibacterial action with relief of the hypoxic wound microenvironment. With tea-leaf-derived exosomes included to steer macrophages toward a reparative state, the dressing accelerated wound closure and blood-vessel formation in diabetic mice; the work is early-stage animal research. Source: [Carbohydr Polym, DOI 10.1016/j.carbpol.2026.125628](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.carbpol.2026.125628) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: day 20 after the PCAC vote — the compounding file stays quiet while the sports-medicine literature delivers its own verdict on the same peptides
timeline.content: Twenty days after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, FDA's own pages remain unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as "before the end of February 2027." What is new this week is scientific rather than regulatory: a UCLA scoping review in The American Journal of Sports Medicine, published August 11, assesses six peptides popular in sports-recovery circles — including BPC-157 and TB-500, which the panel just recommended, and GHK-Cu, which sits in the next review batch — and concludes their claimed musculoskeletal benefits remain unsubstantiated by human trials, with documented risks for some agents (covered separately below). The law firms keep filing their reads: a Holland & Knight client alert stresses that the committee's recommendations are nonbinding, that none of the peptides may lawfully be compounded today, and that FDA can continue enforcement while rulemaking is pending. The industry backdrop is second-quarter earnings, where coverage in CNBC and BioPharma Dive describes a widening divide between Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk in the GLP-1 market (also below). General research only — not medical advice.
