timeline.title: Q2 earnings sharpen the GLP-1 divide: Lilly revenue jumps 48% as Novo discloses CagriSema fell short of tirzepatide in a head-to-head trial
timeline.content: Per CNBC and BioPharma Dive, second-quarter results reported in early August showed Eli Lilly's revenue up 48% to nearly $23 billion, well ahead of estimates, while Novo Nordisk's report disappointed on two fronts: its investigational amylin/GLP-1 combination CagriSema controlled blood sugar less well than Lilly's tirzepatide in a head-to-head trial, and sales of its oral Wegovy fell just short of estimates. Novo also flagged intensifying competition, reduced Medicaid obesity-medicine coverage and lower realized prices under the most-favored-nation pricing agreement. Both companies raised full-year outlooks; markets rewarded Lilly and punished Novo. Source: [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/06/eli-lilly-novo-nordisk-earnings-glp1-market.html), [BioPharma Dive](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/lilly-novo-earnings-2q-2026-wegovy-pill-foundayo-obesity/827027/)

timeline.title: Sports-medicine scoping review of six recovery peptides lands weeks after the FDA panel vote — and finds the human evidence still missing
timeline.content: UCLA orthopaedic surgery researchers, writing in The American Journal of Sports Medicine, systematically reviewed the peer-reviewed literature on BPC-157, TB-500 (thymosin beta-4), CJC-1295, MK-677 (ibutamoren), ipamorelin and GHK-Cu for musculoskeletal recovery. Two-thirds of the identified studies were in animals; human data were sparse, heterogeneous and at best modestly positive, while documented risks included cardiovascular complications and insulin resistance with MK-677. The authors conclude these peptides should not currently be recommended alongside orthopaedic standard of care — a notable data point given two of the six were just recommended for the FDA's 503A compounding list and one is in the next review batch. Source: [Am J Sports Med, DOI 10.1177/03635465261464420](https://doi.org/10.1177/03635465261464420) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two large safety analyses: no significant depression signal on semaglutide in pooled data; GLP-1 class linked to modest laryngeal-symptom risk in 617,296 users
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis in Clinical Obesity pooled trial, observational and pharmacovigilance data and found no statistically significant increase in depression, anxiety or suicidal ideation among patients on semaglutide, though heterogeneity was substantial and the authors frame the result as absence of a detected signal rather than proof of safety. Separately, a TriNetX cohort study in The Laryngoscope of 617,296 GLP-1 users with obesity reported modestly higher six-month odds of cough, foreign-body sensation and voice disorders for most GLP-1 agents — but no signal for tirzepatide — with small absolute risk differences. Source: [Clin Obes, DOI 10.1111/cob.70105](https://doi.org/10.1111/cob.70105), [Laryngoscope, DOI 10.1002/lary.70808](https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.70808) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Real-world files: youth tirzepatide use across three academic centers, and a matched cohort favoring bariatric surgery over semaglutide on cardiovascular events
timeline.content: Two new retrospective analyses add non-trial evidence. In the Journal of Pediatric Endocrinology & Metabolism, a three-center study of 74 patients aged 21 or younger on tirzepatide reported modest BMI reductions and, in those with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c falling from 8.0% to 7.2% with lower insulin requirements. In Endocrine Practice, a TriNetX propensity-matched comparison of bariatric surgery versus semaglutide in adults with obesity found surgery associated with roughly 60% lower risk of a composite cardiovascular outcome over up to five years, in patients with and without diabetes — observational findings subject to residual confounding. Source: [J Pediatr Endocrinol Metab, DOI 10.1515/jpem-2026-0335](https://doi.org/10.1515/jpem-2026-0335), [Endocr Pract, DOI 10.1016/j.eprac.2026.08.006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eprac.2026.08.006) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the second-guessing phase — critics and columnists weigh the PCAC vote while FDA's compounding file stays unmoved
timeline.content: Nineteen days after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon and Semax — for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, FDA's own pages remain unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as "before the end of February 2027," with no date or docket. What has moved is the commentary. A Forbes analysis published August 2 by healthcare-policy writer Joshua Cohen frames the vote as an unusual case of an advisory panel siding against the FDA's own career scientists — who had recommended against all seven substances on characterization, efficacy and safety grounds — and asks how the agency will reconcile the two positions when it decides whether to proceed to rulemaking. That joins the Health Affairs Forefront critique of August 4 warning that a listing would route unapproved substances through pharmacies exempt from routine inspection and adverse-event reporting, and a new law-firm survey of how individual states — California by regulation, Ohio and Washington through board enforcement — are already setting their own guardrails around compounded GLP-1s and peptides regardless of what FDA ultimately decides (both covered separately below). On the research side, no major new trial readouts or journal publications on KB peptides surfaced since yesterday's batch, which covered the pooled semaglutide kidney analysis and several large real-world GLP-1 cohorts. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/joshuacohen/2026/08/02/on-peptides-fda-staff-scientists-at-odds-with-advisory-panel/), [Health Affairs Forefront](https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/fda-advisory-committee-s-vote-may-open-drug-compounding-back-door-unapproved-peptides), [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the compounding file has gone quiet — and the live access fight has moved to a drug nobody can buy yet
timeline.content: Eighteen days after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, FDA's own pages remain unchanged: no proposed rule has published, no Federal Register notice has appeared, and the further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF is still listed only as "before the end of February 2027," with no date or docket. In the absence of movement there, the week's actual access story concerns an investigational drug rather than a compounded one. Per STAT and a report in The BMJ, Eli Lilly confirmed on August 3, 2026 that it will accept applications for early access to retatrutide — its investigational GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist — after it emerged that a single 79-year-old patient had already been granted it, in a request citing refractory obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea and pulmonary hypertension. Coverage in AJMC and Medscape describes clinicians as divided, and notes that the published eligibility criteria are narrow enough that most patients will not qualify; access is not something a patient can request directly, since a treating physician must approach the company, and any supply would still require FDA and institutional review board authorisation. Lilly has said it plans to file a Biologics License Application in the first quarter of 2027. Two things worth separating: an expanded-access programme is a regulated pathway for an unapproved investigational drug supplied by its manufacturer under FDA oversight, which is a different thing entirely from compounding an unapproved bulk substance — and a listing decision on the 503A list, when it eventually comes, concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. Meanwhile the journal literature ran on its own track this week, led by a pooled analysis of three large randomised semaglutide trials reporting reduced major kidney outcomes. This is general research, not medical advice. Source: [STAT](https://www.statnews.com/2026/08/03/eli-lilly-retatrutide-mystery-patient-doctors-seek-same-access-their-patients/), [BMJ, DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100530](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100530), [AJMC](https://www.ajmc.com/view/lilly-expands-retatrutide-access-amid-doctor-pushback), [Medscape](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/retatrutide-expanded-access-draws-mixed-clinician-views-2026a1000qn1), [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — PCAC meetings](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee)

timeline.title: Pooled analysis of SELECT, FLOW and SOUL reports fewer major kidney events on semaglutide across 30,787 trial participants
timeline.content: A prespecified pooled analysis of participant-level data from three large randomised placebo-controlled trials, published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, found that a composite of persistent 50% or greater loss of kidney function, kidney failure, kidney-related death or cardiovascular death occurred as a first event in 973 participants on semaglutide versus 1,134 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.91) over a mean follow-up of roughly three to four years. A narrower composite excluding cardiovascular death was also reduced, and safety outcomes were broadly similar between groups. The authors suggest the effect may not be explained by glycaemic or weight changes alone. The pooled trials differed in population, route and dose, and the analysis was funded by Novo Nordisk with several company-affiliated authors. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00134-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(26)00134-8) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two industry-authored post hoc analyses report better predicted risk scores — for dementia on semaglutide and cardiovascular disease on tirzepatide
timeline.content: Two analyses published the same day both report improvements in modelled future risk rather than in counted clinical events. In Alzheimer's & Dementia, a post hoc analysis of the SELECT trial applied a validated 25-protein plasma dementia risk score to samples from 2,970 adults aged 65 and over at baseline and two years, and found semaglutide slowed the rise in predicted 5-year risk (odds ratio 0.74) and 20-year risk (0.91) versus placebo. In the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, a three-year post hoc analysis of SURMOUNT-1 reported that tirzepatide was associated with a fall in Framingham-equation predicted 10-year cardiovascular risk while placebo was associated with a rise. Neither analysis counted dementia diagnoses or cardiovascular events; both use surrogate endpoints, both are post hoc, and both were authored largely by employees of the respective manufacturers, who state the findings need confirmation in event-based trials. General research only — not medical advice. Sources: [DOI 10.1002/dad2.70432](https://doi.org/10.1002/dad2.70432), [DOI 10.1093/eurjpc/zwag408](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjpc/zwag408) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Network meta-analysis puts the oral GLP-1 agents side by side — and finds no head-to-head data to settle it
timeline.content: A network meta-analysis in Obesity Science & Practice pooled nine randomised trials covering 5,766 adults with overweight or obesity and without diabetes, comparing oral semaglutide, orforglipron, danuglipron and lotiglipron against placebo over 20 to 72 weeks. The higher-dose semaglutide and orforglipron arms showed the largest percentage weight reductions, at roughly 11.6% and 11.8% respectively, with orforglipron producing the greatest absolute weight loss and semaglutide the largest reductions in BMI and waist circumference. The authors rate certainty as low to moderate and stress that no trial has compared these agents directly, so the ranking rests on indirect comparison. Two of the four compounds are discontinued development candidates. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Obes Sci Pract, DOI 10.1002/osp4.70181](https://doi.org/10.1002/osp4.70181) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Real-world analyses look at tirzepatide in 630,545 UK digital-service patients and at GLP-1 drugs in irritable bowel syndrome
timeline.content: Two large database studies published this period sit well outside the trial setting. In Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism, a retrospective cohort of 630,545 adults prescribed tirzepatide through a UK digital service reported mean weight change of −13.5% at six months and −17.4% at twelve months among those with recorded weights, with persistence higher among patients from less deprived areas — though weights were self-reported, only a minority of the cohort had them recorded, and all authors work for the provider being evaluated. Separately, in Digestive Diseases and Sciences, a matched TriNetX analysis of people with irritable bowel syndrome found lower recorded rates of chronic diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain and bloating among those who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist — a direction worth noting given that gastrointestinal intolerance is this class's best-documented side effect. Both rely on coded records and are hypothesis-generating. General research only — not medical advice. Sources: [DOI 10.1111/dom.71067](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.71067), [DOI 10.1007/s10620-026-10171-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10620-026-10171-w) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Law-firm survey: states are writing their own rules for compounded GLP-1s and peptides — California by regulation, Ohio and Washington by enforcement
timeline.content: A Sheppard Mullin analysis, republished by the National Law Review, surveys how states are regulating compounded GLP-1s and peptides "above the federal floor." California has codified compounding regulations, effective October 1, 2025, that tighten the federal "essentially a copy" analysis by requiring pharmacists to verify and document a clinically significant, patient-specific difference before compounding; Ohio and Washington have issued GLP-1-specific pharmacy-board guidance that largely restates federal law but have demonstrated willingness to enforce it. The piece also notes that the twelve peptides removed from FDA's Category 2 list earlier this year remain in a regulatory gray zone — no longer designated a "significant safety risk," but not affirmatively authorized for 503A compounding — and that compounders treating removal as implicit permission carry enforcement risk. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Sheppard Mullin](https://www.sheppard.com/insights/blogs/above-the-federal-floor-how-states-are-regulating-compounded-glp-1s-and-peptides), [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/above-federal-floor-how-states-are-regulating-compounded-glp-1s-and-peptides)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the law firms and pharmacy bodies have filed their read of the PCAC vote — and even the groups that welcomed it are telling members nothing has changed yet
timeline.content: Two weeks after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommended six of seven nominated peptides for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, the second wave of coverage is not news reporting but professional guidance — and it is unusually uniform. Client alerts published in early August by Holland & Knight and by Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney, an analysis from McDermott Will & Emery, a member note from the National Community Pharmacists Association, and explainer coverage from CNN and AJMC all land on the same operative sentence: the recommendations do not authorise anyone to compound these substances today, do not make them FDA-approved drugs, and do not alter the current legal position, because FDA must still decide whether to accept the recommendations and then work through notice-and-comment rulemaking. The Buchanan alert states directly that pharmacies should not interpret the vote as authorisation to begin compounding. Notably, the same caution appears in the statement issued August 4, 2026 by the American Academy of Anti-Aging Medicine and the International Peptide Society — two bodies that welcomed the outcome — which stressed that the vote is advisory and non-binding, that it does not change what is legally permitted to be compounded today, and that the process could extend into 2027 or beyond; readers should note both are membership organisations with a stated interest in broader peptide access, so their framing is a stakeholder position rather than a neutral one. Nothing on FDA's own pages has moved since the last update: no proposed rule has published, and the separately announced further PCAC meeting on Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II and PEG-MGF remains scheduled only as "before the end of February 2027," with no date, docket, or briefing materials posted. A listing concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Holland & Knight](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/08/fda-advisory-committee-endorses-compounding-of-certain-peptides), [Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney](https://www.bipc.com/fda-pcac-recommends-six-peptides-for-the-503a-bulks-list-what-compounding-pharmacies-need-to-know), [McDermott Will & Emery](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/bulk-list-bound-pcac-backs-majority-of-peptides-in-two-day-public-meeting/), [NCPA](https://ncpa.org/newsroom/qam/2026/07/31/fda-advisory-committee-nominates-six-peptides-pharmacies-compound), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/31/health/what-are-peptides-fda-next-steps-wellness), [AJMC](https://www.ajmc.com/view/fda-panel-backs-6-peptides-for-compounding), [A4M / International Peptide Society statement](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/08/04/3338624/0/en/A4M-and-the-International-Peptide-Society-Welcome-PCAC-Recommendations-Supporting-Inclusion-of-Six-Reviewed-Peptides-on-the-503A-Bulk-List.html), [FDA — 503A bulk drug substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act)

timeline.title: BMJ cohort of 52,971 patients reports lower one-year cardiovascular event risk on tirzepatide than on a comparator chosen as a placebo proxy
timeline.content: A population-based cohort study in The BMJ used two national US claims databases and a design previously benchmarked against randomised trials to compare 35,353 people who started tirzepatide with 17,618 who started sitagliptin, all aged 40 and over with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. At one year the weighted risk of major adverse cardiovascular events was 2.9% on tirzepatide versus 4.4% on sitagliptin (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.80; number needed to treat 70), with lower myocardial infarction risk but no meaningful difference in ischaemic stroke. The authors also report lower rates of hospital-treated infection and of all-cause mortality, which they suggest points to mechanisms beyond atherosclerosis. This is observational claims-based research, not a randomised trial, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [BMJ, DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100011](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100011) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Randomised study finds an intermittent schedule that keeps kisspeptin working for 12 days, sidestepping the desensitisation problem
timeline.content: A randomised, single-blinded, placebo-controlled study in the European Journal of Endocrinology tested three kisspeptin-10 administration patterns in 15 healthy men with 12 controls. Continuous infusion over five days left gonadotropin concentrations no different from vehicle — the desensitisation that has limited the field — while a daily intermittent schedule of eight hours on and sixteen hours off sustained increases in luteinising hormone across twelve days, and a challenge bolus afterwards still produced a response, indicating the receptor remained functional. The authors frame the work as protocol development to inform future studies in reproductive disorders. The study is small, short, in healthy volunteers only, and reports no clinical outcomes; kisspeptin is not FDA approved. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Eur J Endocrinol, DOI 10.1093/ejendo/lvag134](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejendo/lvag134) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Systematic review catalogues nerve complications reported alongside rapid weight loss on GLP-1 and dual agonists
timeline.content: A systematic review in the Journal of Neurology searched three databases through 30 June 2026 and identified 19 studies comprising 31 individual cases plus one cohort of 103 people who developed new or worsening peripheral nerve problems while taking weight-loss medications, with all but one study published from 2024 onward. Semaglutide or tirzepatide were implicated in 83% of the individual cases; median weight loss was 21.8% of starting body weight at a median 3.7 kg per month, with symptom onset at a median 150 days, and presentations included fibular neuropathy, lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy and distal symmetric polyneuropathy. The authors urge attention to nutritional status and caution against ultra-rapid weight and HbA1c reduction, while noting explicitly that case reports cannot establish how often this happens. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [J Neurol, DOI 10.1007/s00415-026-14048-w](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00415-026-14048-w) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two HIV-cohort analyses look at semaglutide and smoking, and at semaglutide and mood
timeline.content: Two within-person analyses from the CNICS clinical network were published in AIDS on the same day. One followed 123 people with HIV who smoked at the time they started semaglutide and reported a fall of 2.5 cigarettes per day from an average of 10.5 — a 24% drop in smoking intensity — with 21% reporting not smoking at the end of follow-up. The other tracked PHQ-9 scores in 354 people and found no overall change in depressive symptoms, with a small rise among those who had none at baseline and a larger fall among those with moderately-severe to severe symptoms. Both are uncontrolled observational studies with no comparator group, and semaglutide is not approved for smoking cessation or any psychiatric indication. General research only — not medical advice. Sources: [DOI 10.1097/QAD.0000000000004596](https://doi.org/10.1097/QAD.0000000000004596), [DOI 10.1097/QAD.0000000000004598](https://doi.org/10.1097/QAD.0000000000004598) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Japanese cohort tracks what happens when a national policy forces patients off GLP-1 therapy
timeline.content: A prospective real-world study in Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism followed 104 patients treated under Japan's optimal use guideline, which mandates a six-month lifestyle phase before reimbursed therapy, caps treatment at 68 weeks for semaglutide or 72 weeks for tirzepatide, and then requires a washout. Weight fell to about -16% at the treatment endpoint with the two agents tracking closely from month four onward, but after the mandated stop 95% of patients had regained weight by two months and 83% by six months, with the mean change reverting from -14.4% at month 16 to -7.0% at month 22. The authors question whether a mandated cessation is compatible with the chronic nature of obesity. The study is observational and uncontrolled, with small numbers in the post-cessation windows. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Diabetes Obes Metab, DOI 10.1111/dom.71190](https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.71190) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Health Affairs Forefront: PCAC vote "may open a drug-compounding back door" for unapproved peptides
timeline.content: In Health Affairs' Forefront policy series ("Health Policy at a Crossroads"), an analysis published August 4, 2026 argues that the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee's narrow recommendation to add peptide substances to the 503A Bulks List came despite a lack of demonstrated clinical benefit and substantial safety and quality concerns. The authors note that 503A pharmacies are not required to register with FDA, are not subject to routine inspection, and are exempt from adverse-event reporting requirements — limiting the agency's ability to act quickly on safety signals — and connect the debate to problems already documented with compounded GLP-1 drugs, including insufficient clinician oversight and misleading advertising and promotion. A stakeholder position from the policy-analysis side of the debate, mirroring the industry-side framings logged earlier. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Health Affairs Forefront](https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/fda-advisory-committee-s-vote-may-open-drug-compounding-back-door-unapproved-peptides)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the panel has voted, the rulemaking hasn't started — and the safety literature isn't waiting
timeline.content: Roughly ten days after the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8-6-1 to recommend adding BPC-157, KPV, and TB-500 to the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List (with MOTS-c passing 7-5-2, Semax and Epitalon also recommended, and Emideltide rejected), the practical state of play is unchanged: the votes are advisory, FDA has published no proposed rule, and the agency's own scientists had recommended against all seven. FDA's standing page for the 503A bulks list continues to describe the process as one that runs through notice-and-comment rulemaking before any substance is added, and the agency has separately posted an early announcement of a further PCAC meeting before the end of February 2027 covering Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II, and PEG-MGF. The patient-safety group Partnership for Safe Medicines has argued publicly that the advisory vote risks leaving the impression these unapproved substances are FDA-endorsed. Meanwhile the journal literature indexed in the past few days has continued in a different register from the hearing-room debate: a review summarising rare but potentially irreversible ocular events with GLP-1 drugs, a review describing an EMA pharmacovigilance signal for a lithium interaction, a review finding no generalised neuroendocrine-tumour risk signal, and — for the first time in this feed — a rat study comparing BPC-157 and TB-500 head-to-head. None of that changes any regulatory status. This is general research, not medical advice. Sources: [FDA — Bulk Drug Substances Used in Compounding Under Section 503A](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act), [FDA — July 23-24, 2026 PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/5987510-fda-committee-votes-peptides/), [Partnership for Safe Medicines](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/07/july-27-2026-fda-peptide-panel-narrowly-votes-to-add-unapproved-drugs-to-compounding-list.html)

timeline.title: First head-to-head animal comparison of BPC-157 and TB-500 appears days after the FDA panel voted on both
timeline.content: A rat Achilles tendon study in Joint Diseases and Related Surgery tested BPC-157, TB-500, and the two together after standardised tendon transection and repair. TB-500 was the only group to reach a statistically significant biomechanical advantage at four weeks, both peptides improved histopathological scores relative to controls, and combining them produced no additional benefit over either alone. The study is preclinical, exploratory, and in eight animals per group; the authors call for dose-optimisation and longer follow-up. Source: [DOI 10.52312/jdrs.2026.2951](https://doi.org/10.52312/jdrs.2026.2951) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Review flags rare irreversible eye events with GLP-1 drugs and urges baseline ophthalmic assessment in high-risk patients
timeline.content: A review in the Journal of the Association of Physicians of India summarises postmarketing signals linking GLP-1 receptor agonists and tirzepatide to worsening diabetic retinopathy and to non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, a rare but potentially irreversible cause of sudden vision loss. The authors note the WHO and the European Medicines Agency now recognise NAION as a very rare adverse effect of semaglutide, that a class effect is being explored, and that causality remains unproven; they call for baseline ophthalmic evaluation in high-risk individuals and stronger pharmacovigilance. Source: [DOI 10.59556/japi.74.1507](https://doi.org/10.59556/japi.74.1507) (PubMed)

timeline.title: A separate review describes an EMA pharmacovigilance signal for a GLP-1 and lithium interaction
timeline.content: A review in International Clinical Psychopharmacology counts six distinct reports since 2025 of lithium elevation or toxicity following initiation, switching, or escalation of GLP-1 or dual incretin agonists in bipolar disorder, and states that the European Medicines Agency's Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee opened a signal in June 2026 for a drug interaction leading to increased lithium levels. The authors separate the uncontrolled signal from mechanistic plausibility and note that the most obvious explanations are quantitatively insufficient; this is a review of case-level reports and does not establish causation. Source: [DOI 10.1097/YIC.0000000000000636](https://doi.org/10.1097/YIC.0000000000000636) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two real-world cohorts add non-trial evidence on semaglutide in children and tirzepatide in adults
timeline.content: A nationwide Icelandic retrospective cohort in Pediatric Obesity followed 113 children aged 12 and over prescribed subsidised semaglutide and reported that a longstanding upward weight trajectory reversed on treatment, with 63% achieving a reduction exceeding 10 percentage points on the study's BMI measure. Separately, a prospective Spanish cohort of 107 adults in Clinical Nutrition ESPEN reported a mean 17.21% weight reduction at six months on tirzepatide with a 3.7% dropout rate. Both are observational and uncontrolled. Sources: [DOI 10.1111/ijpo.70139](https://doi.org/10.1111/ijpo.70139), [DOI 10.1016/j.clnesp.2026.105005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clnesp.2026.105005) (PubMed)

timeline.title: CBC investigation reports Canadian doctors routing patients to an unauthorised peptide through a compounding gap
timeline.content: A CBC News investigation, summarised in the outlet's Marketplace briefing of August 2, 2026, reports that Health Canada prohibits BPC-157 from being sold as an injectable drug or licensed as a natural health product, but that it can be compounded in oral form by a pharmacy on a physician's prescription — a route the broadcaster says some clinics are using to supply it. Journalists using hidden cameras visited advertised clinics in Ontario and British Columbia; Health Canada told CBC that BPC-157 has not been authorised, that its safety, efficacy and quality have not been assessed, and that scientific evidence supporting its use is limited. University of Alberta health-law professor Timothy Caulfield is quoted saying physicians should be warning patients about these products rather than providing them. The report sits alongside Health Canada's standing advisory against unauthorised injectable peptides bought online and a June 2026 permanent injunction obtained against a Canadian retailer. General research only — not medical advice. timeline.title: This week in peptides: the question FDA kept asking and nobody answered — when a prescription says "TB-500," what is actually in the vial?
timeline.content: A detailed account of day two of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting, published July 28, 2026 by the regulatory law firm Hyman, Phelps & McNamara, shifts the focus from the vote tallies to the characterisation problem FDA pressed throughout both days. Per that account, an FDA scientist likened the exercise to buying a car for a teenager and ending up with "a Volvo with NASCAR racecar specs" — the same nameplate over a different amino-acid count and molecular weight — and noted that "TB500" typically refers to a 17-amino-acid fragment but that exact sequences and molecular weights vary between vendors, asking the panel, "When you write a script for TB500, what form do you think your patients are receiving?" The agency told the committee it lacks authority to define what these common-name substances are; that none is an FDA-approved drug and any clinical investigation would require an Investigational New Drug application; that 503A compounders are not required to report adverse events, so the agency does not receive that data; and that the panel should treat the absence of information as its own data point. FDA also corrected a common framing, with the acting director of its Office of Compounding Quality and Compliance describing a listing not as restoring prior access but as "creating" legal access for the first time. Two further details for the record: all industry nominations had been withdrawn in the months before the meeting, and FDA asked members not to weigh that in their votes. On what happens next, the same analysis notes FDA has confirmed this proceeds as notice-and-comment rulemaking in which it will analyse the full record — so the proposed rule, not the panel's recommendations, is where this is resolved — and floats an interim option of enforcement discretion conditioned on requirements such as adverse-event reporting and sourcing, grading, identification and release testing of bulk substances. Note that published vote counts for one substance differ slightly between outlets; the committee's recommendations remain advisory and non-binding either way, and a listing concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [FDA Law Blog / Hyman, Phelps & McNamara (day two)](https://www.thefdalawblog.com/2026/07/the-peptide-l-wave-rolls-on-pcac-adds-two-more-bulk-drug-substances-for-the-503a-list/), [FDA Law Blog (day one)](https://www.thefdalawblog.com/2026/07/peptide-l-wave-pcac-approves-four-bulk-drug-substances-for-the-503a-list/), [FDA.gov PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026), [FDA 503A bulk substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act)

timeline.title: Phase 2 trial of oral semaglutide in alcohol use disorder published in the American Journal of Psychiatry
timeline.content: A phase 2 double-blind randomised trial in 50 treatment-seeking adults with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder reported that oral semaglutide did not significantly reduce the primary endpoint — laboratory-measured alcohol cue-elicited craving — or drinks per day, but was associated with significant reductions in heavy drinking days, drinks per drinking day, naturalistic craving, cannabis use days, and alcohol-related consequences over eight weeks. The authors say the results echo earlier findings in non-treatment-seekers and support continued development. The trial is small and short, and semaglutide is not approved for alcohol use disorder; a separate Department of Veterans Affairs Phase 3 study in this indication was registered days earlier. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [American Journal of Psychiatry, DOI 10.1176/appi.ajp.20260003](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.20260003) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two new Phase 3-stage registrations extend GLP-1 testing into knee osteoarthritis and acute stroke care
timeline.content: Two trial registrations posted to ClinicalTrials.gov push incretin-class agents further outside their approved metabolic indications. NCT07734311, sponsored by Hangzhou Sciwind Biosciences, is a Phase 3 placebo-controlled study of the investigational GLP-1 receptor agonist ecnoglutide in 360 participants with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, with a listed start date of 31 July 2026. NCT07734792 is a Phase 2/3 randomised, blinded-outcome study of tirzepatide versus standard medical care for functional outcomes in 430 patients with acute ischaemic stroke undergoing endovascular thrombectomy, with a listed start date of 10 August 2026. Both are registrations only — neither has reported results, and neither use is FDA approved. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07734311](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07734311), [NCT07734792](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07734792)

timeline.title: European Heart Journal study links a GLP-1 receptor agonist to a protective endothelial pathway in preclinical pulmonary hypertension
timeline.content: A study in the European Heart Journal reports that an AMPK/USP10 feedback loop in lung endothelium helps maintain levels of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and lung vascular patency, and that this loop is suppressed in human idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and in rodent models. Mice treated with the GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide showed mitigated pulmonary hypertension comparable to genetically modified mice, which the authors present as a rationale for studying GLP-1 receptor agonists in pulmonary arterial hypertension. The work is preclinical and mechanistic and has not been tested in humans for this purpose. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [European Heart Journal, DOI 10.1093/eurheartj/ehag568](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag568) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Novo Nordisk signals it will seek a court order halting Eli Lilly's comparative GLP-1 advertising
timeline.content: Days after filing a federal lawsuit in New Jersey alleging that Eli Lilly's direct-to-consumer advertising for Zepbound and Mounjaro makes misleading comparative claims, Novo Nordisk notified the court that it intends to file a motion for a preliminary injunction on August 17, 2026 — an escalation that would seek to halt the advertising while the case proceeds rather than waiting for a final judgment. Novo's complaint centres on comparisons that it says omit a higher-strength version of Wegovy approved earlier in 2026. Lilly has denied wrongdoing and said it stands by its advertising. This is a commercial advertising-law dispute between two manufacturers of FDA-approved medicines and does not itself change any approval or clinical recommendation. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Fierce Pharma](https://www.fiercepharma.com/marketing/novo-turns-heat-lilly-false-advertising-suit-seeking-preliminary-injunction-stop-rivals), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2026/07/24/novo-nordisk-eli-lilly-lawsuit-weight-loss-drug-ads.html), [STAT](https://www.statnews.com/pharmalot/2026/07/21/novo-nordisk-sues-eli-lilly-glp1-drug-ads/)

timeline.title: Case series flags anhedonia-like symptoms in three patients on higher-dose tirzepatide
timeline.content: A three-patient case series in Obesity Pillars describes women treated for obesity at or near maximal tirzepatide dosing who reported reduced motivation, emotional flatness, or loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities despite successful weight loss, with symptoms improving after dose reduction and, in one patient, recurring when the previous level was resumed. The authors hypothesise a link to modulation of mesolimbic dopaminergic pathways and suggest monitoring for changes in motivation during treatment. A three-patient series is the weakest form of clinical evidence and cannot establish how often, or whether, this occurs. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Obesity Pillars, DOI 10.1016/j.obpill.2026.100302](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obpill.2026.100302) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Two preclinical skin studies revisit LL-37 and GHK-Cu
timeline.content: Two laboratory studies published this period looked at peptides already covered in this knowledge base in the context of skin inflammation. A study in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences tested an injectable polymer against rosacea-like inflammation driven by excessive LL-37, reporting reduced inflammatory signalling in keratinocytes and a smaller lesion area in an LL-37-injected mouse model. Separately, a study in Antioxidants reported that a formulated combination of a plant extract with GHK-Cu suppressed Th2 cytokine transcription and promoted keratinocyte migration in a cell model of atopic dermatitis. Both are preclinical — cell-culture and animal work — and neither was tested in people. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Int J Mol Sci, DOI 10.3390/ijms27146425](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27146425), [Antioxidants, DOI 10.3390/antiox15070818](https://doi.org/10.3390/antiox15070818) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the margins were narrow — and the make-up of the panel that produced them is now part of the story
timeline.content: With the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) votes of July 23–24, 2026 now on the record, the detail drawing scrutiny is how close they were and who cast them. Per trade coverage citing Reuters, BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 each cleared on an 8-in-favour, 6-against vote with one abstention, and MOTs-C passed 7–5 with two abstentions — majorities of one or two members, not consensus. The votes also ran against the agency's own reviewers, who had recommended against expanding compounding access for all seven nominated substances, citing limited safety and effectiveness data; FDA officials used the hearing to note that compounded products carry no required labelling on dosing or risk and to urge sponsors toward formal applications and controlled human trials. Reporting notes that seven of the committee's fourteen members were added ahead of the meeting from clinics or businesses that sell peptide treatments, and that most members voting in favour have industry ties. A HHS spokesperson said all committee members underwent the same ethics review and vetting required of any FDA advisory committee member. Not every panellist was persuaded: committee member Elizabeth Rebello of the University of Texas said, "I'm concerned that we're responding to a market-induced demand rather than a decision based in solid science." The practical position is unchanged — the agency is not bound by its advisers, has issued no final determination, and any listing would run through notice-and-comment rulemaking; a listing concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Pharmaceutical Technology](https://www.pharmtech.com/view/peptide-compounding-vote-raises-questions-drug-developers), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/fda-panel-votes-place-popular-peptide-bpc-157-compounding-list-2026-07-23/), [FDA PCAC meeting page](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026)

timeline.title: Novo Nordisk sues Eli Lilly over GLP-1 comparative advertising
timeline.content: Novo Nordisk filed a federal lawsuit against Eli Lilly on July 21, 2026, alleging that Lilly's direct-to-consumer advertising for Zepbound and Mounjaro misleads patients by making comparative claims against Wegovy and Ozempic while omitting the higher-strength version of Wegovy that the FDA approved in March 2026. Novo's complaint argues that because no head-to-head trial has compared the highest strengths of the competing products, comparisons that leave out the newer approved strength are misleading. Eli Lilly defended its advertising as based on what it describes as the strongest available scientific evidence. The dispute is a commercial and advertising-law matter between two manufacturers of FDA-approved GLP-1 medicines and does not itself change any approval or clinical recommendation. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/21/novo-nordisk-sues-eli-lilly-glp-1-ads.html), [Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/07/21/glp-1-ad-war-leads-lawsuit-by-novo-nordisk-claiming-eli-lilly-misleads/), [PharmExec](https://www.pharmexec.com/view/novo-nordisk-sues-eli-lilly-glp-advertising-alleging-misleading-dosing-comparisons)

timeline.title: Real-world preprint reports weight change on tirzepatide and semaglutide below landmark-trial figures
timeline.content: A retrospective cohort preprint posted to medRxiv analysed 13,507 adults in a US telehealth obesity programme and reported a mean six-month weight loss of 11.5%, with 59.1% of patients reaching at least 10% total body weight loss. After propensity-score matching, patients using tirzepatide reached that 10% threshold 18.1 percentage points more often than those using semaglutide. The authors stress that these real-world figures sit meaningfully below the averages reported in the landmark randomised trials and that their six-month readout is not time-matched to those 68- and 72-week endpoints. The work is observational, drawn from a single telehealth platform, authored by contractors for that company, and has not been peer reviewed. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [medRxiv, DOI 10.64898/2026.07.14.26357502](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.14.26357502)

timeline.title: New Phase 3 registrations appear for amycretin, CagriSema in adolescents, and semaglutide in alcohol use disorder
timeline.content: Several Phase 3 trial registrations relevant to the GLP-1 and amylin classes have been posted to ClinicalTrials.gov. Novo Nordisk's AMAZE 7 (NCT07668414) is registered as a head-to-head comparison of once-weekly zenagamtide — the naming applied to the investigational GLP-1/amylin co-agonist amycretin — against once-weekly semaglutide in participants with overweight or obesity, with a planned 650 participants and a September 2026 start. A separate Novo trial (NCT07282613) extends CagriSema into children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes. Independently, the US Department of Veterans Affairs registered CSP #2041 "CRAVE" (NCT07218354), a placebo-controlled Phase 3 study of semaglutide in Veterans with alcohol use disorder, with a planned 622 participants. All three are registrations only — none has reported results, and none of the investigational uses is FDA approved. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07668414](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07668414), [NCT07282613](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07282613), [NCT07218354](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07218354)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the calendar already turns to the NEXT peptide review — FDA lists five more substances for a meeting before the end of February 2027
timeline.content: Two days after the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) finished voting on the first seven nominated research peptides, the more consequential detail for the months ahead is the one sitting on FDA's own advisory-committee pages: the agency has posted an early announcement that it will host another PCAC meeting **before the end of February 2027**, and the published agenda names five additional bulk drug substances being considered for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List — Cathelicidin (LL-37), GHK-Cu, Dihexa acetate, Melanotan II, and Mechano Growth Factor, Pegylated (PEG-MGF). Four of those five are already covered as monographs in this knowledge base; PEG-MGF is not, and is flagged here as a candidate for future coverage. Per the FDA notice, the meeting time and location have not yet been scheduled, no Federal Register notice or public-comment docket has published yet, and meeting materials are expected no later than two business days beforehand — so the substantive signal on FDA's scientific position on these five is still months away. Context to keep straight on the July round: the committee's six-of-seven vote is advisory and non-binding, and under FDA's 503A interim policy the agency publishes a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking upon completing its evaluation, meaning any listing runs through notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than taking effect from the vote. A listing decision concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [FDA.gov PCAC February 2027 meeting announcement](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [FDA.gov 2027 meeting materials](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee/2027-meeting-materials-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee), [RAPS / Regulatory Focus](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-considers-adding-a-dozen-peptides-to-its-bulk-drug-compounding-list.html), [FDA 503A bulk substances](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/bulk-drug-substances-used-compounding-under-section-503a-fdc-act)

timeline.title: Nature Metabolism study maps separate brain regions behind GIP receptor activation versus blockade
timeline.content: A mouse study published in Nature Metabolism reports that two anatomically distinct brain regions appear to explain a long-standing puzzle in metabolic pharmacology — why adding either a GIP receptor agonist or a GIP receptor antagonist to GLP-1 receptor agonism can each produce additional weight loss. Using region-selective genetic knockouts, the authors report that the area postrema mediates appetite suppression from GIP receptor agonism, while hypothalamic GIP receptors underlie the ability of GIP receptor antagonism to enhance the effect of GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonists. The work is preclinical and has not been tested in humans, but it bears on the mechanism of dual-agonist and amylin-based agents such as tirzepatide and cagrilintide. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Nature Metabolism, DOI 10.1038/s42255-026-01575-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42255-026-01575-z) (PubMed)

timeline.title: Meta-analysis reports semaglutide more than doubled odds of MASH resolution, with fibrosis effect still uncertain
timeline.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized trials, published in Medicine (Baltimore), pooled data on semaglutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and steatohepatitis. Semaglutide was associated with a more than doubled likelihood of steatohepatitis resolution without fibrosis progression (risk ratio 2.14) and with reductions in liver enzymes, body weight, and glycated hemoglobin, while improvement in fibrosis stage was not statistically significant. Gastrointestinal adverse events and treatment discontinuation were more frequent than with placebo, with serious adverse events comparable; the authors graded the fibrosis finding as uncertain and called for longer, adequately powered trials. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [Medicine (Baltimore), DOI 10.1097/MD.0000000000049916](https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000049916) (PubMed)

timeline.title: This week in peptides: the PCAC has voted — panel backs 6 of 7 peptides for the 503A list, rejects Emideltide, and the FDA now decides
timeline.content: At the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting that concluded July 24, 2026, the panel voted to recommend adding six of the seven nominated research peptides to the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, overriding the FDA's own career scientists, who had recommended against all seven. On July 23 the committee backed BPC-157 (nominated for ulcerative colitis) and KPV (wound and inflammatory conditions) by 8–6 with one abstention, along with TB-500 and MOTS-c (MOTS-c by a narrower 7–5, two abstentions). On July 24 it backed Epitalon (nominated for insomnia) 7–5 with one abstention and Semax (cerebral ischemia, migraine, trigeminal neuralgia) 8–5, while rejecting Emideltide (DSIP) — nominated for insomnia, narcotic dependence, and opioid withdrawal — in a 6–7 vote with one abstention. Reporting frames the outcome as aligned with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stated support for broader peptide access. Context to keep straight: the votes are advisory and non-binding — the FDA makes the final determination through notice-and-comment rulemaking, which commentators note can take many months, and a listing decision concerns compounding eligibility, not FDA approval of a drug. Separately, BPC-157 came off the FDA's Category 2 "do-not-compound" list effective April 23, 2026 (removal is not authorization to compound), and the agency's proposal to exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list remains in post-comment review. General research only — not medical advice. Source: [RAPS / Regulatory Focus (day two)](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-advisory-committee-backs-two-more-peptides-rejects-one-for-compounding-list.html), [RAPS / Regulatory Focus (day one)](https://www.raps.org/resource/fda-advisory-committee-backs-two-controversial-peptides.html), [STAT](https://www.statnews.com/2026/07/23/fda-panel-okays-peptides-compound-pharmacies-bpc-157-kpv/), [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/5987510-fda-committee-votes-peptides/), [FDA.gov PCAC meeting](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/july-23-24-2026-meeting-pharmacy-compounding-advisory-committee-07232026)
